# Prescriptive lessons -- pat-martino x linear-expressions

## m7

Martino's entire system treats the minor seventh chord as the atomic unit of melodic decision-making: the chord's inversion form -- not the player's ear or the key signature -- is the operative selector for which activity to play. Position on the neck carries a separate, independent meaning: the same form shape moved up the neck changes the key, not the activity. The system is designed to be traversed cyclically, with Activities 1 and 5 sharing Form 1 and the same starting pitch, and mastery across all twelve keys horizontally is a hard prerequisite before any vertical (Phase II) work begins.

- [ch.1 p.10] Identify the m7 chord's inversion form (1-4); that form number directly selects the corresponding activity (Form 1 -> Activities 1 or 5, Form 2 -> Activity 2, etc.). Melodic choice follows from inversion, not from independent judgment.
- [ch.1 p.11] Position on the fingerboard is the key selector: the same activity shape at third position = G minor, fifth position = A minor, and so on. The form itself is key-neutral; position assigns the key.
- [ch.1 p.15] After Activity 5, cycle back to Activity 1 an octave higher rather than stopping -- Activities 1 and 5 share Form 1 and the same sixth-string root (G), making the system infinitely repeatable up the neck.
- [ch.1 p.16] [PROSCRIPTIVE] Do not advance to Phase II (vertical movement) until all five activity forms are mastered in all twelve keys horizontally. The text states this non-negotiably: "Then and only then should you move onto PHASE II."

---

## maj7

Martino handles maj7 by collapsing it into the relative minor, eliminating any need for a separate melodic vocabulary. The substitution is direct: Cmaj7 = Am9, applying the activities system without modification.

- [ch.3 p.50] Substitute the relative minor seventh for any maj7 chord (Cmaj7 -> Am9). This single reduction makes the entire minor-based activities system applicable to major seventh chords with no additional machinery.

---

## maj9

Martino offers a secondary substitution path for maj9 when the primary relative minor is harmonically less desirable, routing through the III chord of the major key instead.

- [ch.3 p.50] For maj9 chords, optionally substitute the secondary relative minor (the III chord of the major key): Cmaj9 -> Em7. Use this when the primary relative minor (Am7) creates harmonic friction in context.

---

## maj6

Martino treats maj6 as the clearest case of relative-minor equivalence -- the pitch content is identical, making the substitution direct with no voice-leading adjustment required.

- [ch.3 p.50] Substitute the relative minor seventh directly for any maj6 chord (Cmaj6 -> Am7). The two chords share all pitch content; no adjustment is needed beyond renaming the root.

---

## maj (slash chords)

For major triads appearing over a foreign bass note, Martino applies a two-tier decision tree: primary relative minor first, secondary relative minor (III of the major key) as fallback when the bass note creates a b5 against the primary substitute. The b5 interval clash is the explicit disqualifying test.

- [ch.4 p.56] Convert the major triad to its relative minor; reinterpret the bass note as a scale degree of that minor key (C/F# -> Am, F# treated as the 6th of A minor).
- [ch.4 p.56] [PROSCRIPTIVE] Do not apply the primary relative minor when the bass note creates a b5 against the substitute minor root -- this interval clash is the disqualifying condition requiring fallback.
- [ch.4 p.56] When the primary relative minor is disqualified by a b5 bass clash, fall back to the secondary relative minor (III chord of the major key). For Db/E: Bb minor is rejected (E = b5 against Bb); F minor (III of Db major) is prescribed. Validate by confirming the minor scale contains all pitch content of the slash chord.

---

## dom7

Martino collapses the entire dominant quality family -- C7, C9, C13 -- into a single category and resolves all of them to a minor form rooted a perfect fifth above the dominant root. The target form is specifically m6, not plain m7.

- [ch.4 p.55] Treat C7, C9, and C13 as quality-equivalent. Convert to the minor sixth form rooted a perfect fifth above the dominant root (G9 -> Dm6). This closes the three-way substitution loop among m7b5, m6, and dominant ninth.

---

## dom7alt

Martino handles altered dominants with a single half-step-up rule for substitution and an explicit scale prescription that pits melodic minor against harmonic minor -- harmonic minor is rejected because it omits the b7, the defining tone of the dominant seventh.

- [ch.4 p.57] Move up one half-step from the dominant root and play minor (Gb7 altered -> G minor). This single directional instruction converts the altered chord into a form the activities system handles directly.
- [ch.4 p.57] Prefer melodic minor over harmonic minor as the scale over an altered dominant -- only melodic minor contains the b7, the essential "hot" note of the dominant seventh sound.
- [ch.4 p.57] [PROSCRIPTIVE] Do not use harmonic minor as a first-choice scale over an altered dominant: although it yields b9, #9, b5, and #5, it lacks the b7, making it an insufficient and weaker substitute for melodic minor.

---

## m7b5

Martino grounds the m7b5 substitution in a specific inversional identity -- m7b5 is not approximated by m6, it *is* m6 in third inversion -- and the interval formula (up a minor third, play minor) follows directly from that structural equivalence.

- [ch.4 p.55] Move up a minor third from the m7b5 root and play minor (Bm7b5 -> Dm6). The rationale is structural: m7b5 is an incomplete dominant ninth and is Dm6 in third inversion, so the substitution is harmonically exact.
- [ch.4 p.55] Understand the bi-directional inversion equivalence: Bm7b5 = Dm6 in third inversion; Dm6 = Bm7b5 in first inversion. This identity is the conceptual foundation for the substitution rule and confirms that the same activities apply across both chord types without approximation.

---

## m6

Martino uses m6 as the preferred output form when reducing dominant ninths, and treats m6 and m7b5 as freely interchangeable through their shared inversional identity.

- [ch.3 p.50 / ch.4 p.55] Treat m6 and m7b5 as freely interchangeable within the substitution system (Dm6 = Bm7b5 in first inversion; Cm7b5 = Ebm6). Neither chord type requires separate melodic treatment.
- [ch.4 p.55] When reducing a dominant ninth, target the m6 form -- not plain m7 -- as the output: G9 -> Dm6 (minor rooted a perfect fifth above the dominant root). The m6 form is specifically preferred.

---

## aug

Martino treats the augmented triad as an enharmonic multiplier: because all three inversions of an augmented triad are themselves augmented triads (F aug = A aug = Db aug), each chord yields three distinct minor-maj7 substitution targets from a single major-sixth-up rule.

- [ch.4 p.55] Before applying any substitution, identify all three enharmonic root names of the augmented triad (F aug = A aug = Db aug). Treating each note as a valid root is the prerequisite step.
- [ch.4 p.56] Go up a major sixth from each enharmonic root and play minor-maj7 (preferring melodic minor): F aug -> Dm(maj7), using F; -> F#m(maj7), using A; -> Bbm(maj7), using Db. A single augmented triad thus opens three distinct minor-maj7 substitution paths.
